strengths: Introduction of a novel and physically grounded multi-agent benchmark: Moving Out fills a clear gap between discrete grid-world environments (e.g., Overcooked-AI) and rigid cooperative carrying setups by offering continuous control, dynamic collision/friction interactions, varied physical attributes (mass, shape, size), and distinct coordination modes.

Comprehensive human dataset collection: The authors collected over 1,000 human demonstrations across 36 participants for behavior diversity and 720 expert demonstrations for physical attribute variation, complete with IRB approval and fair participant compensation.

Well-motivated method tailored to multi-agent physical interaction: BASS leverages sensible multi-agent data augmentations (partner pose perturbation and sub-trajectory recombination) and couples them with latent world model rollouts for test-time action selection, showing consistent empirical gains across multiple base models (GRU and Diffusion Policy).

Extensive evaluation including human-in-the-loop testing: Beyond self-play and AI-AI evaluations, the authors conducted an interactive user study with real human partners, supplemented by detailed ablation studies, latency analysis, and failure mode categorization.
weaknesses: Discrepancy in human subject participant reporting: In Section 6.1, the manuscript states that the human subject study was conducted with 32 participants, whereas Appendix I.1 explicitly states 'In total, we conducted this experiment with 12 volunteers.' This inconsistency regarding sample size needs clarification.

Legibility and presentation of core experimental figures: Figure 6 is poorly scaled, with tiny axis labels, legends, and overlapping error bars that make it extremely difficult to parse quantitative differences directly from the main body without consulting the supplementary tables.

Reliance on hand-crafted distance heuristics for action selection: The simulation and action selection mechanism relies on evaluating candidate actions against an engineered metric (Normalized Final Distance computed via 2D BFS). This restricts the action selection component to navigation/delivery tasks where distance metrics to goals can be explicitly computed.

Simplifications of 2D planar physics: Although a step forward from discrete gridworlds, the 2D top-down physics engine (Pymunk) still abstracts away complex real-world manipulation challenges such as 3D grasp stability, out-of-plane torque, and occlusion.

strengths: Addresses an important and practical gap in human-AI collaboration by moving beyond discrete gridworlds (e.g., Overcooked) and rigidly bound setups into a physically grounded continuous 2D environment with collision dynamics, friction, and heterogeneous object attributes.

The Moving Out benchmark is well conceptualized, featuring 12 carefully designed maps categorized into three distinct collaboration modes (Coordination, Awareness, and Action Consistency) alongside two well-defined evaluation tasks.
Comprehensive empirical evaluation combining AI-AI evaluations, ablation studies, failure case analyses, and a real-time human-AI interactive user study.
The proposed BASS framework demonstrates consistent performance gains across both tasks and against strong baselines including Diffusion Policy and MAPPO.
weaknesses: The algorithmic novelty of BASS is somewhat limited: pose jittering and trajectory swapping/stitching are established data augmentation techniques, while the simulation and selection module is effectively a standard 1-step greedy model-predictive action filter.

Myopic 1-step action evaluation: scoring actions based solely on 1-step predicted progress (NFD reduction toward the goal) could easily suffer in environments with complex obstacles or narrow corridors where agents must temporarily move away from the goal or maneuver jointly around corners.

Inconsistency in user study description: Section 6.1 of the main text states that 32 participants took part in the human subject study, whereas Appendix I.1 states 'In total, we conducted this experiment with 12 volunteers.' This discrepancy should be clarified.

Presentation flaws: Figure 6 is cramped with very small fonts, making the comparison bars and error bars difficult to parse without high magnification. Additionally, the project URL in the abstract ends abruptly without a link.

strengths: Addresses an important gap in human-AI collaboration research by moving beyond discrete grid-world setups (e.g., Overcooked-AI) into a continuous, 2D physics-grounded environment with forces, friction, collisions, and geometric constraints.

Provides a well-categorized benchmark of 12 maps spanning three distinct collaborative modes (coordination, awareness, and action consistency), accompanied by a dataset of human-human interaction demonstrations.

The proposed BASS framework introduces intuitive and effective domain-specific improvements: partner pose perturbation and sub-trajectory recombination for data augmentation, alongside a latent dynamics model for test-time action candidate evaluation.

Comprehensive empirical evaluation that incorporates both AI-AI self-play and interactive human-in-the-loop experiments, supported by ablations across multiple backbone architectures (GRU and Diffusion Policy) and qualitative failure mode analysis.
weaknesses: There is a notable discrepancy in reporting the human study participant count: Section 6.1 states that the study was conducted with 32 participants, whereas Appendix I.1 states that the experiment was conducted with 12 volunteers. This inconsistency needs clarification.

The baseline comparisons do not fully isolate the benefit of test-time planning: BASS pairs the generative policy with a 1-step latent dynamics model and distance-to-goal scoring, effectively acting as model-predictive action filtering. Baselines like Diffusion Policy do not appear to receive a comparable action reranking/filtering mechanism.

Comparison with MAPPO is inherently asymmetric: MAPPO is trained from scratch via RL with dense reward engineering and without human demonstrations, whereas the BC baselines and BASS directly leverage human demonstration data. Known human-compatible RL baselines (e.g., Fictitious Co-Play or BC-regularized RL) are omitted.

Scalability and collision validity of the trajectory recombination augmentation are not thoroughly analyzed: matching continuous poses across sub-trajectories requires discretization into a 48x48 grid, and it is unclear how frequently valid matches occur or how often swapped partner trajectories create physically invalid overlaps/collisions in more congested maps.
Presentation polish issues, including an incomplete sentence with an empty project link at the end of the Abstract ('The project page is available at ') and minor grammatical slips in the main text.

strengths: Addresses an important limitation in human-AI collaboration research by moving beyond discrete/symbolic grid-worlds (e.g., Overcooked-AI) into a physically grounded, continuous state-action environment with continuous force alignment, object geometry, and friction.

Substantial dataset collection and rigorous experimental protocol: collected over 1,000 human-human trajectories across 12 maps from 36 participants for behavioral adaptation, alongside 720 trajectories for physical attribute generalization, with appropriate IRB approval.

Well-designed method (BASS) tailored to multi-agent physical coordination, featuring multi-agent sub-trajectory stitching/augmentation, latent dynamics modeling, and sample-based action selection using task progress (NFD).

Thorough evaluation combining reproducible cross-group AI-AI proxies, comprehensive ablation studies across model components and backbones, and direct human-in-the-loop user studies with both objective metrics and subjective Likert feedback.
weaknesses: There is an unresolved discrepancy in the reported number of human study participants: Section 6.1 states that the study evaluated BASS against DP with 32 participants, whereas Appendix R.1 states that the experiment was conducted with 12 volunteers. This inconsistency should be clarified.

The environment is based on a top-down 2D physics simulation (Pymunk/Magical). While it introduces continuous dynamics, grasping and friction, claims regarding 'embodied AI' and real-world robotics are somewhat overstated given the lack of 3D kinematics, realistic contact dynamics, and occlusion.

The simulation and action selection relies on a 1-step lookahead heuristic based on Normalized Final Distance (NFD). While BFS helps handle static wall navigation, 1-step greedy planning may struggle with dynamic deadlocks or non-monotonic cooperative manipulation tasks, and extending beyond 1-step could be computationally prohibitive under real-time constraints.

strengths: Addresses an important and timely problem: bridging the gap between discrete/grid-world human-AI benchmarks (e.g., Overcooked-AI) and physically-grounded continuous multi-agent collaboration requiring fine-grained force alignment and spatial coordination.

Substantial data collection effort: The authors collected over 1,000 human-human interaction demonstrations across 36 participants for behavioral diversity (Task 1) and 720 expert demonstrations across randomized physical attributes (Task 2), under an IRB-approved protocol.

Technically coherent method (BASS): The combination of boundary-matched multi-agent trajectory recombination (preserving goal consistency while expanding partner behavior coverage) and latent dynamics simulation with partner action inference offers an effective mechanism for online action filtering.

Thorough evaluation: The paper evaluates models across multiple dimensions (TCR, NFD, WT, AC), tests both seen and unseen participant splits as reproducible proxies, and validates findings with interactive human-AI user studies and qualitative failure case analysis.
weaknesses: Discrepancy in human user study reporting: Section 6.1 states that the interactive human study was conducted with '32 participants', whereas Appendix R.1 states 'In total, we conducted this experiment with 12 volunteers.' This inconsistency must be clarified, as it directly impacts the interpretation of sample size and the reported statistical tests (e.g., p = 0.017).

Myopic 1-step action selection: Action selection evaluates candidate actions by rolling out the learned dynamics model for only a single step ($z_{t+1}$) using Normalized Final Distance (NFD). In complex physical environments with obstacles and narrow passages, greedy single-step distance reduction can be prone to local minima (e.g., pressing an object against an intervening wall). A discussion or ablation regarding multi-step rollout horizons versus inference latency at 10 Hz would strengthen the methodology.

Interaction between Action Chunking and Selection: Diffusion Policy typically predicts temporal action chunks (horizons of 8 steps with 4 executed, as noted in Appendix J.2). It is not completely clear in Section 5.2 whether BASS scores the immediate next transition ($t+1$) or the culmination of the action chunk, and how candidate multi-step trajectories are evaluated by the latent dynamics model.

Baseline comparability for RL: MAPPO is trained from scratch with dense distance-based shaping, which struggles heavily in continuous continuous spaces due to exploration bottlenecks, whereas behavior cloning baselines leverage rich human demonstrations. Benchmarking against a human-guided or demonstration-initialized RL baseline (e.g., offline RL or BC pretraining + RL fine-tuning) would provide a fairer comparison for the RL paradigm.

strengths: Relevant and timely problem formulation: Moving beyond discrete, symbolic grid worlds (such as Overcooked-AI) into continuous, physically grounded multi-agent coordination with force alignment, mass, and shape constraints is an important step for embodied human-AI collaboration.

Comprehensive benchmark and real human dataset: The authors developed 12 diverse layouts categorised across three coordination modes (coordination, awareness, action consistency) and collected substantial human demonstration data (>1,000 trajectories across 36 participants in Task 1, and 720 expert trajectories under randomized object physical properties in Task 2) with IRB approval.

Thoughtful algorithmic design (BASS): The framework sensibly tackles multi-agent imitation learning challenges via boundary-consistent sub-trajectory recombination, partner state perturbation, and partner-conditioned latent dynamics rollout for multi-candidate action selection.

Thorough experimental ablations: The supplementary material provides detailed ablations investigating individual modules (Table 5), candidate sampling sizes and combinations (Table 8), comparisons against oracle simulation (Table 4), and alternative dynamics architectures (Table 11).
weaknesses: Inconsistency in reported human study participant numbers: In Section 6.1 (page 8), the paper states: 'We conducted a human subject study with 32 participants to evaluate BASS against the DP baseline in both tasks.' However, in Appendix R.1 (page 27), the text states: 'In total, we conducted this experiment with 12 volunteers. Each volunteer will be paid $20 for one hour of playing.' This discrepancy is concerning and requires immediate clarification.

Myopic 1-step action selection: Action candidate evaluation relies on a single-step lookahead evaluated with Normalized Final Distance (NFD). Although a 2D BFS distance map is utilized to mitigate immediate wall obstacles, 1-step greedy selection can struggle in scenarios requiring coordinated multi-step manoeuvres (e.g., backing up or reorienting an irregularly shaped object before turning a tight corner).

Simplifications of 2D planar physics: While the paper positions itself as advancing physically grounded embodied collaboration, the simulation environment is built upon a 2D rigid-body engine (Pymunk/Magical). The dynamics (top-down 2D sliding/pushing) do not fully capture 3D embodied robotic manipulation challenges (e.g., 6-DoF grasping, balance, occlusion), which should be clearly scoped.

Uneven baseline comparison with from-scratch RL: MAPPO is trained from scratch with dense heuristic rewards and struggles significantly with continuous exploration. Given that the focus is on adapting to human demonstrations, comparing against human-aligned RL or offline RL baselines (e.g., BC-initialized RL or offline multi-agent RL) would provide a more rigorous baseline comparison.
